Step 2: munged encodes a short credential holding the numeric UID and GID, drawn as a small token card with a clock icon labelled validity window, five minutes by default. Step 3: a green arrow labelled credential sent with the request crosses the gap from the left munged to the right munged. Step 4: inside the right box, munged decodes the credential, and an arrow leads out from it to a result box labelled numeric UID and GID reported back. Below both node boxes sits one wide key box labelled /etc/munge/munge.key, with a note beside it reading same key on every node. Two dotted lines run from the key box up into each munged box. Orange highlight on the key box, the single most important item. Number circles 1 to 4 mark the steps in time order. Green takeaway bar at the bottom: This is how Slurm can trust user 1042 sent this without passwords.
alt: Munge encodes a credential on the sending node and the controller decodes it with the same shared key.
cap: Munge lets the controller trust a user ID because every node decodes the same credential with one shared key.

name: h07-bringup-order
title: First bring-up order for a new Slurm cluster
spec: A left-to-right chain of eight numbered step boxes, arranged in two rows of four with an arrow from the end of row one down to the start of row two. Each box has a green number circle with its step number 1 to 8 and a small outline icon, then a bold title and a short line of text. Step 1, title Users and time: create the slurm and munge users with fixed, identical UIDs on all nodes; confirm chrony is synchronised. Step 2, title Munge: create the key on one node, copy it to all nodes with mode 0400 and owner munge, then test with munge -n | unmunge. Step 3, title Database: install MariaDB, create the slurm_acct_db database and the slurm user. Step 4, title slurmdbd: write slurmdbd.conf with mode 600 and owner slurm, start it, and read its log because it creates the tables on first start. Step 5, title Controller: put slurm.conf in /etc/slurm, create the state and log directories owned by slurm, start slurmctld. Step 6, title Compute nodes: start slurmd on each node, copy the config or use configless mode. Step 7, title Accounting hierarchy: run the sacctmgr commands. Step 8, title Verify: run sinfo, scontrol ping, and sacct. Each arrow goes from one step to the next, and every step is drawn in the same size box. Above the row of boxes, a short orange note reads each step depends on the one before it. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads Order matters when you bring a cluster up for the first time.
alt: Eight numbered steps bring up a Slurm cluster in order, from users and munge through the database and daemons to verification.
cap: A first Slurm install works in eight ordered steps, and each one depends on the step before it.

name: h07-upgrade-order
title: Upgrade order: database, controller, then nodes
spec: A horizontal chain of three large boxes left to right with arrows between them. Box 1 titled slurmdbd, with a small database cylinder icon, labelled database first. Box 2 titled slurmctld, with a gear icon, labelled controller second. Box 3 titled slurmd and clients, with a server icon, labelled nodes last. Number circles 1, 2 and 3 sit on the boxes in time order. Above the chain, a box with a shield icon lists the two steps before you start: take a database backup, copy StateSaveLocation. Beneath the chain, a note reads stay within the supported compatibility window. Orange highlight on the arrow between box 2 and box 3. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads Reversing that order is how a rolling upgrade turns into a stuck cluster.
alt: Slurm upgrades go in order: slurmdbd first, then slurmctld, then slurmd and the clients.
cap: Upgrade slurmdbd first, then slurmctld, then the compute nodes and clients, so no daemon meets a message it cannot read.

name: h10-task-remap
title: A job sees its GPUs renumbered from zero
spec: Three columns from left to right. Left column: a node box titled gpu node with eight small GPU boxes in one row, labelled /dev/nvidia0 through /dev/nvidia7. Only /dev/nvidia3 and /dev/nvidia7 are filled green and marked allocated; the other six are light grey with a small padlock icon, and a bracket under the grey boxes reads hidden by ConstrainDevices=yes. A caption under the node box reads the cgroup exposes /dev/nvidia3 and /dev/nvidia7. Middle column: a single box labelled SLURM_JOB_GPUS=3,7, with an arrow from the green GPUs into it. Right column: two task boxes stacked vertically with a note that they run with --gpus-per-task=1. Task 0 box reads CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 and below it a small label reads physical GPU 3. Task 1 box reads CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 and below it a small label reads physical GPU 7. Thin arrows run from the middle box to each task box, labelled relative to the job. Number circles are not used. Orange highlight on the relative-to-the-job label, the single most important point. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads The job sees a renumbered world, so scripts should follow the renumbering, not the physical labels.
alt: Allocated GPUs 3 and 7 appear inside the job as CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES 0 and 1, one for each task.
cap: Inside a job, the allocated GPUs are renumbered from zero, so physical GPU 3 can appear as device 0.

name: h10-numa-binding
title: GPU and CPU binding on a two-socket node
spec: A two-socket node drawn as one wide outline. Left half: a box titled Socket 0, NUMA 0, with a label Cores=0-31 and a row of four GPU boxes labelled GPU 0, GPU 1, GPU 2, GPU 3. Right half: a box titled Socket 1, NUMA 1, with a label Cores=32-63 and a row of four GPU boxes labelled GPU 4, GPU 5, GPU 6, GPU 7. Below the node, a row of three option cards side by side, each with a small outline icon. Card 1 title: --gpu-bind=closest. Text: each task is bound to the nearest GPU, with CPUs from the same NUMA node. Card 2 title: --gres-flags=enforce-binding. Text: CPUs come only from the cores bound to the job's GPUs, and the job may wait longer. Card 3 title: --gres-flags=disable-binding. Text: any core on the node can be used, for a job that wants more CPUs than its GPUs have bound to them. A thin dashed line from card 1 points to the socket that holds the chosen GPU. The card 2 border is orange as the single most important item. Below the cards, a small note reads check the layout with nvidia-smi topo -m. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads Bind when ranks need their GPUs close to their CPUs, and confirm the layout first.
anchor: ## 3. Binding GPUs to tasks and CPUs
alt: On a two-socket node, GPUs 0 to 3 sit on socket 0 with cores 0 to 31, and GPUs 4 to 7 sit on socket 1 with cores 32 to 63.
cap: On a two-socket node, each GPU has a local socket, so binding keeps a rank's CPUs and GPU on the same side.

name: h10-sharing-spectrum
title: Sharing one GPU trades isolation for density
spec: A horizontal arrow across the top of the figure, labelled more isolation on the left and more density on the right. Above the arrow, a separate box at the far left labelled Whole GPU, the default for training, with a note never share, and an icon of one full GPU block. Below the arrow, three cards placed left to right in increasing density order: card 1 MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) with an icon of a GPU split into blocks, note hardware partitioned, strong isolation, static layout, no NVLink across slices. Card 2 MPS (Multi-Process Service) with an icon of several small processes on one GPU, note several processes share one GPU, a percentage of GPU resources each, no memory isolation, trusted users only. Card 3 Sharding with an icon of a clock dividing time into slices, note takes turns on a GPU, does not fence processes or constrain device memory by default. Each card has a bold title and a short line of text, with the same size boxes. The card 2 box has the orange highlight as the single most important item for shared work. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads Each sharing method trades isolation for density, so choose by what the workload can tolerate.
anchor: ## 5. Sharing a GPU: MIG, MPS and sharding
alt: Whole GPUs, MIG, MPS and sharding sit on a spectrum from strong isolation to high density.
cap: Each way of sharing a GPU gives up some isolation to fit more jobs on one device.

name: h11-batch-vs-steps
title: Commands without srun run once, on the first node
spec: Two panels side by side. Left panel titled Batch script, with a short script box listing three lines in monospace: echo Start, then srun hostname, then echo End. Above the script box, two directive lines in monospace: #SBATCH --nodes 2 and #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node 2. Right panel titled Allocation of two nodes, with two large node boxes stacked vertically. The top node box is labelled n10 and carries a green badge reading Step 0, first allocated node. The bottom node box is labelled n11. Arrow 1: from the echo Start line to the top node box only, with a label runs once. Arrow 2: from the srun hostname line to both node boxes. Inside the top node box, two small task blocks, each labelled n10. Inside the bottom node box, two small task blocks, each labelled n11. A caption under the task blocks reads runs four times across the two nodes, in arbitrary completion order. Arrow 3: from the echo End line to the top node box only, labelled runs once. Below the right panel, a dashed note box with an orange border reads without srun, the second node stays idle. Number circles are not used. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads A command without srun runs once, on the first node.
alt: In a two-node batch script, echo lines run once on the first node, while srun hostname runs four tasks across both nodes.
cap: In a multi-node batch script, only the lines that start with srun reach the second node.

name: h11-array-grid
title: Mapping array task 5 onto a learning-rate and batch-size grid
spec: A grid drawn as a table with four columns and three rows. Column headers across the top, left to right: learning rate 1e-4 (LR index 0), 3e-4 (LR index 1), 1e-3 (LR index 2), 3e-3 (LR index 3). Row labels down the left side, top to bottom: batch size 16 (BS index 0), batch size 32 (BS index 1), batch size 64 (BS index 2). Each cell shows its array task number in a green square: row 16 holds tasks 0, 1, 2, 3; row 32 holds tasks 4, 5, 6, 7; row 64 holds tasks 8, 9, 10, 11. The cell for task 5, in the row for batch size 32 and the column for 3e-4, has the orange highlight. Beside the grid, a small arithmetic panel with three lines in monospace: LR_IDX = 5 % 4 = 1, BS_IDX = 5 / 4 = 1, pair = (3e-4, 32). Under the grid, a note reads %4 throttle: four training runs read the dataset at once, and the other eight wait. Number circles are not used. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads Modulo picks the learning rate, and integer division picks the batch size.
anchor: ### 2D hyperparameter grid search with job arrays (*Distributed AI Systems* Chapter 8)
alt: Array task 5 maps to learning rate 3e-4 and batch size 32 using modulo and integer division.
cap: Each array task index maps to one learning rate and one batch size, so task 5 runs 3e-4 with batch size 32.

name: h11-dependency-chain
title: A training run split across segments, then evaluated
spec: A left-to-right chain of three job boxes with arrows between them. Box 1, labelled J1, train segment 1, with a small script icon labelled train.sh. Box 2, labelled J2, train segment 2, resumes from latest checkpoint, with a script icon labelled train.sh. Box 3, labelled J3, evaluate, with a script icon labelled evaluate.sh. Arrow from J1 to J2, labelled --dependency=afterany:$J1, with a note beneath reading a timeout counts as a failure, so afterany lets the chain continue. Arrow from J2 to J3, labelled --dependency=afterok:$J2, with a note beneath reading the evaluation runs only if segment 2 succeeds. Number circles 1, 2 and 3 mark the boxes in time order. Below box 2, an orange-bordered note box reads if a job with afterok fails, the dependent job stays pending with DependencyNeverSatisfied; add --kill-on-invalid-dep=yes to cancel it instead. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads Each segment resumes from the latest checkpoint, so no work repeats.
alt: Two training segments run one after another with afterany, and an evaluation job runs with afterok after the last segment.
cap: Dependencies chain training segments and an evaluation job so the run continues past one time limit.

name: h11-signal-requeue
title: A warning signal, a clean stop, and a requeue
spec: Three swim lanes drawn as horizontal bands, top to bottom: Batch shell (the script), Training (srun python train.py), slurmctld (controller). Time flows left to right. Number circles mark steps in time order. Step 1, in the batch shell lane: an arrow arrives labelled #SBATCH --signal=B:USR1@600, with the note 600 seconds before the time limit, the batch shell receives USR1. Step 2, in the batch shell lane: a box labelled trap runs checkpoint_and_requeue. Step 3, arrow from the batch shell lane to the training lane, labelled kill -TERM on the training process, with a note that the training program writes a checkpoint on SIGTERM. Step 4, in the batch shell lane after the wait: a box labelled wait for training to exit. Step 5, arrow from the batch shell lane up to the slurmctld lane, labelled scontrol requeue $SLURM_JOB_ID. Step 6, in the slurmctld lane: a box labelled job goes back to the queue with the same job ID. A small note in the slurmctld lane reads the next run sees SLURM_RESTART_COUNT increase. The step 5 arrow is orange as the single most important item. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads Periodic checkpoints are the real safety net; the signal handler saves the wait for the next checkpoint.
alt: At a warning signal, the batch shell stops the training process, waits for it to exit, and requeues the job with the same ID.
cap: A warning signal lets the batch script stop training cleanly and requeue the job under the same ID.

name: h12-launch-styles
title: Two launch styles: srun per GPU or torchrun per node
spec: Two panels side by side, each titled with its style. Left panel title: Style A, srun with one task per GPU. A top box labelled srun python train.py, with arrows fanning out to four node boxes labelled node 1 to node 4. Each node box holds a row of eight small rank boxes, one per GPU. A label under the left panel reads Slurm starts every rank. Right panel title: Style B, one torchrun per node. A top box labelled srun torchrun, with arrows to four node boxes labelled node 1 to node 4. Each node box holds one wide torchrun box, and inside it a row of eight small rank boxes started by torchrun. A label under the right panel reads Slurm sees one task per node. Below both panels, a comparison strip with two rows of short text. Row for Style A: Slurm keeps control of binding, cgroups, accounting per step and signals; train.py reads SLURM_PROCID, SLURM_LOCALID and SLURM_NTASKS. Row for Style B: torchrun adds elastic features and sets the rank variables for you; the cost is coarser per-rank binding and GPU isolation. Orange highlight on the label Slurm sees one task per node, the single most important item. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads Pick the launch style before you write the batch script, because the training code has to match it.
alt: Style A starts every GPU rank from srun, while style B starts one torchrun per node that launches the eight local ranks.
cap: Style A lets Slurm start every GPU rank, while style B lets torchrun start the ranks on each node.

name: h12-glue-translation
title: Translating Slurm variables into PyTorch variables
spec: Two columns of boxes with a narrow translation band between them. Left column, titled Slurm variables, five boxes top to bottom: SLURM_PROCID (global task number), SLURM_LOCALID (position on its own node), SLURM_NTASKS (total number of tasks), SLURM_JOB_NODELIST (compressed nodelist), SLURM_JOB_ID (job number). Right column, titled PyTorch variables, five boxes in the same top-to-bottom order: RANK, LOCAL_RANK, WORLD_SIZE, MASTER_ADDR, MASTER_PORT. Five horizontal arrows run straight across the middle band, one per row, each labelled with its rule: the first row labelled global task number, the second labelled position on node, the third labelled total tasks, the fourth labelled first host in the nodelist, the fifth labelled 10000 plus job ID modulo 20000. The arrows are parallel and do not cross. In the middle band, above the arrows, a small box labelled dist_env() holds the rule set. Beneath the MASTER_ADDR and MASTER_PORT boxes, a dashed loop arrow labelled a value already set in the environment wins. The fifth arrow (MASTER_PORT) has the orange highlight as the single most important rule. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads The glue only maps variables; it does not prove the network is fast.
alt: Five Slurm variables map straight across to RANK, LOCAL_RANK, WORLD_SIZE, MASTER_ADDR and MASTER_PORT.
cap: The glue maps five Slurm variables onto the PyTorch rendezvous variables, and a value you set yourself wins.

name: h12-master-addr-trap
title: A loopback MASTER_ADDR splits one job into isolated groups
spec: Two panels side by side. Left panel title: MASTER_ADDR set to 127.0.0.1. Two node boxes, node A and node B, drawn apart with no connection between them. Each node box holds its own group box labelled 1-node process group. A dashed double-headed line between node A and node B is crossed out with the note gradients are never synchronized across nodes. A status note under the left panel reads training looks normal and does not crash. Right panel title: MASTER_ADDR from the first host in the nodelist. The same two node boxes, now both with arrows pointing into one wide shared box labelled one process group across both nodes. The shared box shows a sub-label first host in the nodelist. Orange highlight on the two isolated groups in the left panel, the single most important item. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads Derive MASTER_ADDR from the nodelist, and never use 127.0.0.1 on a multi-node job.
alt: A MASTER_ADDR of 127.0.0.1 gives each node its own process group, while the first host in the nodelist joins all nodes into one group.
cap: Setting MASTER_ADDR to 127.0.0.1 on a multi-node job splits it into separate single-node groups that never sync gradients.

name: h12-diagnose-ladder
title: Diagnosing the fabric in three rungs
spec: A vertical ladder with three rungs stacked from the bottom up, each rung a wide box with a green number circle and an outline icon. Rung 1 at the bottom, titled Reachability: each node pings the others, command srun -N 2 bash -c echo hostname and ping. Rung 2 in the middle, titled AllReduce sweep: tensor sizes 1, 10, 100 and 500 MB, with 3 warmup calls and 10 timed calls, and a formula line bandwidth = (size_mb * 2 * 10) / elapsed. Rung 3 at the top, titled Point-to-point latency: 100 round trips of a one-element tensor between rank 0 and the target, with a formula line one-way latency = (elapsed / 200) * 1e6 microseconds. An arrow on the left side runs up the ladder labelled work from small to large. A note beside rung 1 reads If this fails, nothing above it can work. Beside rung 3 is a short branch note: low bandwidth means bisect the node list with exclude. Orange highlight on rung 1, the single most important rung. Green takeaway bar at the bottom reads Test reachability first, then bandwidth, then latency.
alt: A three-step check tests node reachability, then AllReduce bandwidth across sizes, then point-to-point latency.
cap: Check node reachability first, then all-reduce bandwidth, then point-to-point latency, because each step depends on the one below.
